title: Ashtpadi 10, salok: countless
hook: the salok marvels at countless beings

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi nine: Singh and Kaur, and a badge set down. Your line was substance over title. Today, ashtpadi ten, and the camera pulls back. Day four hundred seventy-four.

Rush hour at a train station. A flood of people, every one of them the main character of their own story. One is late for a job interview. One just got engaged. One is going to visit a mother in hospital. One is humming. You'll never know any of them, and each one carries an inner life as large as yours. A crowd like that can make a person feel very small, or strangely tender. For several ashtpadis, Sukhmani has zoomed in on one kind of person. Now it pulls back, and looks at the crowd.
screen: `A STATION AT RUSH HOUR.` → `EACH ONE A WHOLE STORY.` → `SUKHMANI PULLS BACK.`

segments.voice: The salok of ashtpadi ten has two lines. The first: ustat karahi anek jan. Countless people sing His praise. Ustat is praise; anek is many, more than one can number. And there's no end, no far shore, to it. Ant na paaraavaar: no end, no near bank or far bank. The second line: Nanak, God made the creation in so many ways, of countless kinds. Rachnaa is creation, the thing made, the way a poem or a building is made. Bahu bidh, many ways. Anik prakaar, countless kinds. Notice what's being praised here. Not one perfect person. Not the brahm giaanee of two ashtpadis ago. The sheer number and variety of what exists. In the stanzas that follow, Guru Arjan will list them: people who worship and people who wander, scholars and the lost, worlds beyond worlds. The salok sets the tone for all of it, and the tone is wonder. So many. That's the whole carry, two words, and it's enough. Because when you really take in so many, something shifts. Your own problems are still real, but they're one story among millions. The people who annoy you are also among the so many, each with a whole inner life. And the One who made the creation in all those ways, the salok says, is beyond any shore you could reach. In this salok, the crowd isn't a reason to feel lost. It's a reason for wonder, and everyone in it is part of the same creation.
screen: `USTAT: COUNTLESS PEOPLE PRAISE.` · `NO END, NO FAR SHORE.` · `RACHNAA: A CREATION OF MANY KINDS.` · `ONE STORY AMONG MILLIONS.` · then, large: `SO MANY.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at a crowd kindly. If you can, look out a window at people passing, or at faces in a photo, or, eyes closed, picture a busy street you know. Pick out one stranger. Imagine, just for a breath, that they too woke up this morning with worries and hopes. Then another. Then another. Let your face soften as you look. You don't need to know their names. If you pray, you can wish them well in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Rachnaa, the creation, the thing made. Its salok marvels at countless people praising, and a rachnaa made in so many ways.
Your line: so many. Next time you're in a line or a crowd today, look up, and let the two words go through your mind. Day four hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani Sahib meet this salok at the opening of the tenth ashtpadi, whose stanzas go on to list the countless beings of the creation.

fork.setup: you're in a huge crowd and feel tiny. by the tenth salok, what's another way to see it?
options: you're one story among so many, all part of one creation.
everyone else matters less than you.
fork.reveal: the salok's tone is wonder: so many, made in so many ways.

original.note: Gurmukhi: rachnaa, creation, the thing made; God made it, the salok says, in countless kinds.

trapdoor: what you thought: so many people makes each one matter less.
what it means: the salok's response to the countless is wonder, not shrinking.
what a scholar hears: paaraavaar (paar, the far bank + avaar, the near bank) is a Gurbani idiom for limit; ashtpadi ten's stanzas build on it with the refrain 'kaee kot'.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
